strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing VLM-based IQA methods (Q-Insight, VisualQuality-R1) are single-pass and text-only, lacking mechanisms for iterative visual verification analogous to how humans zoom in to inspect quality-relevant regions.

The GR-IQA dataset curation pipeline is a thoughtful attempt to solve the hard problem of grounding holistic IQA judgments in specific regions without expensive human annotation, using two complementary filters (Visual Reliance Filtering for image-dependency and Hint-Augmented Consistency Filtering for hallucination detection using low-level quality hints).

The KL-Coverage regularizer is a well-motivated technical contribution that targets a concretely diagnosed failure mode (severe 'score collapse' in RL-trained IQA models, e.g., VisualQuality-R1's 2.04% unique score ratio vs. 71.34% ground truth), and the ablation (Table 3, rows 4 vs 5) shows consistent gains from it.

Evaluation is fairly comprehensive: score regression across 7 datasets spanning in-the-wild, synthetic, and AI-generated distortions; a VLM-as-judge protocol for assessing reasoning quality along four axes; and a downstream image-restoration application demonstrating practical utility of the generated reasoning as guidance prompts.

Qualitative examples (Figs. 1, 4, 10-13) are detailed and illustrate the intended hypothesize-crop-verify behavior clearly, including cases where competing methods make factually incorrect claims that Zoom-IQA avoids or corrects via its zoom mechanism.
Thorough ablation study isolating the contributions of SFT, score/rank rewards, KL-Coverage loss, and progressive resampling.
weaknesses: The core score-regression results (Table 1) show only marginal or comparable performance relative to non-reasoning SOTA methods like DeQA-Score, which outperforms Zoom-IQA on most benchmarks (e.g., KonIQ 0.953 vs 0.938, SPAQ 0.895 vs 0.900 close, LiveW 0.892 vs 0.887). The claimed superiority is restricted to comparison against other 'reasoning' baselines, which somewhat narrows the practical significance of the numerical improvement.

The reasoning-quality evaluation (Table 2) relies exclusively on VLM-as-judge scoring (Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-5-mini), with no human study to validate that these automatic judgments align with actual human quality perception; this is a potential source of bias, especially since the training data itself (GR-IQA) was also generated by a closely related Gemini model, raising concerns about evaluator-generator similarity effects.

The GR-IQA dataset is relatively small (~7,000 trajectories), and its full construction and filtering pipeline depends on proprietary/closed-source APIs (Gemini-2.5-pro, Qwen-2.5-32B-based HACF), which may hinder exact reproducibility and independent verification of data quality.

Restoration experiments (Figs. 5, 7-9) are purely qualitative; no quantitative image quality metrics (e.g., no-reference IQA scores, LPIPS versus references, or user study) are reported to substantiate the claim of 'far superior restoration,' making the downstream application evidence largely anecdotal.

There is no analysis of the added inference-time computational cost or latency introduced by the multi-turn crop-and-verify process relative to single-pass baselines, which is relevant for practical deployment.

The paper does not report how often/accurately the model correctly decides 'easy case' vs. 'hard case' (i.e., precision/recall of the crop-triggering policy), which is central to the claimed self-guided exploration contribution but is not directly evaluated.

No variance/statistical significance reporting across runs or datasets, and some ablation gains (e.g., KADID, PIPAL rows in Table 3) are inconsistent or non-monotonic across components, which is not discussed.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and under-explored gap in VLM-based IQA: existing reasoning-based IQA methods (Q-Insight, VisualQuality-R1) generate single-pass text-only reasoning without any mechanism to verify claims against image evidence; the proposed iterative crop-and-verify pipeline is a sensible and well-motivated solution.

The GR-IQA dataset curation pipeline (Visual Reliance Filtering + Hint-Augmented Consistency Filtering) is a thoughtful attempt to mitigate hallucination in VLM-generated CoT rationales without relying on token-level log-probabilities (unavailable for closed-source generators), and is clearly documented with concrete filtering examples in the supplementary.

The KL-Coverage regularizer is grounded in an empirically observed and quantified failure mode (VisualQuality-R1's 2.04% unique score ratio vs. 71.34% ground truth), giving a clear motivation for the design rather than an ad hoc fix; the ablation (Table 4) shows consistent, if modest, gains from this component.

Comprehensive experimental protocol: score regression across seven diverse IQA benchmarks (in-the-wild, synthetic, AI-generated), reasoning-quality evaluation with two independent closed-source VLM judges plus a supplementary human study and a third judge (Grok) to rule out self-preference bias, a downstream restoration application with two restoration frameworks, a dedicated saliency-grounding benchmark, and thorough ablations isolating each proposed component (rewards, KL-coverage, progressive resampling, cropping policy vs. center-crop heuristic, RL vs. single-stage SFT).

Reasonable technical formulation combining format/score/rank rewards (Thurstone-model-based ranking) with GRPO, and clear documentation of prompts/pipelines in the supplementary material aiding reproducibility understanding.

Qualitative examples (Figs. 1, 4, 10-13) convincingly illustrate cases where competing single-pass methods make factually incorrect or incomplete quality claims that the proposed zoom-and-verify mechanism corrects.
weaknesses: The core score-regression results (Table 1) are mixed rather than clearly state-of-the-art: Zoom-IQA underperforms DeQA-Score on nearly every dataset and is not uniformly better than Q-Insight/VisualQuality-R1 (e.g., KADID PLCC 0.701 vs. Q-Insight's 0.702/VisualQuality-R1's 0.703; AGIQA SRCC 0.765 vs. Q-Insight's 0.766). The paper's claim of 'consistently superior performance' against reasoning-based baselines is only partially supported by the numbers shown.

The restoration downstream evaluation (Table 3) is similarly mixed — Zoom-IQA has the lowest PSNR on DIV2K/SUPIR among compared methods, and the paper's narrative selectively highlights the metrics where it wins (best CLIPIQA, best MANIQA under SUPIR, best NIQE/MUSIQ under DreamClear) without fully engaging with metrics where it does not lead.

Reasoning-quality evaluation relies heavily on VLM-as-judge scoring by Gemini-2.5-Flash, the same model family used to generate the GR-IQA training data and rationale filtering (also via Gemini-2.5-pro), raising a self-preference/circularity concern; while the supplementary partially addresses this with a Grok evaluator and a small human study (15 annotators, 30 images), this important control is relegated to the appendix rather than being central to the main paper's claims.

The apparent 'iterative' region reasoning is effectively limited to at most two turns (initial pass + a single crop-and-verify pass); the method does not appear to support genuinely multi-step iterative refinement despite the framing suggesting an open-ended iterative process.

The GR-IQA dataset is relatively small (~7,000 trajectories) and generated entirely from a single source dataset (KonIQ) using a closed-source, potentially non-reproducible and costly API (Gemini-2.5-pro), which raises reproducibility concerns and questions about how well the grounded-rationale behavior generalizes beyond KonIQ-style content.

Method novelty is somewhat incremental at the algorithmic level: the two-stage SFT+GRPO pipeline, reward design (format/score/rank), and RL stabilization tricks build directly on established recipes from Q-Insight/VisualQuality-R1/entropy-collapse literature; the primary novel elements are the crop-action mechanism and the dataset curation modules, whose contribution to raw scoring accuracy (vs. Q-Insight/VisualQuality-R1) is modest per Table 1.

The saliency grounding benchmark (Table 6) evaluates only the proposed model versus its own un-fine-tuned backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7b), without comparison to Q-Insight/VisualQuality-R1's own region attention/grounding behavior if any, making it hard to assess whether the grounding advantage is unique to Zoom-IQA or simply a consequence of any fine-tuning.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated gap: existing VLM-based IQA reasoning methods are single-pass and lack visual grounding/interactivity, while the paper's crop-and-zoom mechanism is a natural fit for how humans actually inspect image quality.

The GR-IQA dataset construction pipeline is carefully engineered with two non-trivial filtering modules (VRF and HACF) that specifically target hallucination in generated rationales, an issue that is often ignored when using strong VLMs (e.g., Gemini) to auto-label reasoning data.

The KL-Coverage regularizer is motivated by a concrete, quantified failure mode (severe score-diversity collapse in VisualQuality-R1, 2.04% vs. 71.34% unique-score ratio) and is shown via ablation (Table 4) to give consistent gains across nearly all benchmarks.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this type of work: score regression across 7 datasets, VLM-as-judge reasoning quality evaluation with two independent evaluators plus a third evaluator (Grok) and a human study to rule out self-preference bias, a dedicated Saliency Grounding Benchmark (Table 6) to verify that zoomed regions are semantically meaningful rather than arbitrary, and a downstream restoration application across two different restoration frameworks and datasets.

Ablations are comprehensive and isolate the contribution of each proposed component (SFT, score/rank rewards, KL-Coverage loss, progressive resampling, RL vs. single-stage SFT, learned zoom vs. center crop), giving good evidence that the design choices are individually justified rather than just the sum working well.

Reasonable attention to reproducibility/practicality concerns: inference-time overhead is quantified and shown to be modest (~0.06s vs. 0.02-0.05s for baselines), and the supplementary discussion proactively addresses edge cases (bokeh, night-time noise) that could otherwise be seen as failure modes of a crop-based pipeline.
weaknesses: The core score-regression results (Table 1) are only "comparable" to prior VLM-based methods and are frequently matched or slightly beaten by non-reasoning scoring methods like DeQA-Score, and are essentially tied (sometimes slightly worse) compared to Q-Insight/VisualQuality-R1 on several datasets (e.g., KADID PLCC 0.701 vs 0.702/0.703, AGIQA PLCC 0.816 vs 0.816/0.817). The paper's central quantitative claim of superiority over reasoning baselines is thus somewhat overstated relative to the actual margins.

The downstream restoration results (Table 3) are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: Zoom-IQA has the worst PSNR under SUPIR and is not best on MANIQA under DreamClear, which weakens the claim of consistently superior real-world applicability, even though CLIPIQA and a few other metrics favor the method.

There is a potential circularity concern in the reasoning-quality evaluation: the GR-IQA training data is generated by Gemini-2.5-pro, and one of the two primary judges in the main paper (Table 2) is Gemini-2.5-Flash from the same model family; while the supplementary adds a third evaluator and human study, this should ideally have been foregrounded in the main text rather than relegated to supplementary material.

GR-IQA contains only ~7,000 reasoning trajectories curated from a single dataset (KonIQ), which is a relatively small and single-source basis for the SFT stage; the extent to which this limits generalization to substantially different distortion types or domains (e.g., heavily synthetic or AI-generated distortions) is not deeply analyzed.

Reliance on a closed-source, expensive-to-query VLM (Gemini-2.5-pro) plus a large auxiliary LLM rater (Qwen-2.5-32B) for the entire data-curation pipeline creates a non-trivial reproducibility/cost barrier for other researchers wishing to replicate or extend GR-IQA construction.

The zero-shot generalization claim would be strengthened by explicit quantitative comparison against other "zoom-style" IQA baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., DOG-IQA), which are discussed qualitatively but not benchmarked numerically against Zoom-IQA.
